The assessment, compiled by the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights in collaboration with local partners, documents the persistent gaps in assistance for civilians affected by successive wars that began with the 1979 Soviet invasion, continued through the civil strife of the 1990s, the Taliban regime, and the 2001 U.S.-led intervention.

The report finds that many survivors lack basic medical care for injuries and trauma, face unemployment and poverty, and are excluded from legal mechanisms that could provide compensation or acknowledgment of their suffering. It calls on the Afghan authorities, international donors and humanitarian agencies to establish comprehensive support programs, ensure accountability for violations, and create a transparent reparations framework. The UN urges that addressing these unmet needs is essential for fostering long‑term stability and reconciliation in a country still grappling with the legacy of prolonged conflict.
author: UN News

title: UN chief urges SCO to support more representative global governance
content:
UN Secretary‑General António Guterres on Tuesday called on the leaders of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) to play a constructive role in reshaping global governance as the international system adapts to new challenges. Speaking at a summit of the SCO, the UN chief argued that a more genuinely multipolar order would reinforce multilateralism, promote fairness and better address the needs of developing nations.

Guterres highlighted the SCO’s growing influence across Eurasia and urged its members to cooperate with existing institutions to ensure that decision‑making reflects a broader range of perspectives. He said that coordinated action among major powers and regional blocs could help balance geopolitical interests, improve the effectiveness of global responses to crises, and create a more inclusive framework for sustainable development. The appeal underscores the United Nations’ push for broader participation in shaping international rules and norms.
author: UN News

title: US airstrikes on Iranian wedding near Sirik kill at least five
content:
A series of U.S. airstrikes near the town of Sirik on Iran’s southern coast on Thursday wounded dozens of civilians and claimed at least five lives, according to Iranian officials.  The strikes reportedly struck a wedding ceremony that was underway in the area, with reports indicating that the attack hit a gathering of family members and guests who had assembled for a celebratory event.  The Iranian Ministry of Health confirmed the casualty figures and said that emergency services were dispatched to the site.

Iran’s government has condemned the attack as an unprovoked assault on civilians and has called for an international investigation.  The incident follows a pattern of escalating tensions between Tehran and Washington, with both sides accusing each other of provocative military actions over the past months.  U.S. officials have not yet released a statement regarding the operation, but the event has intensified calls for restraint amid ongoing regional instability.

The Iranian authorities have announced that they will review the circumstances surrounding the attack and seek accountability for the loss of civilian life.  Meanwhile, diplomatic channels remain open as both nations weigh the implications of the strike for broader U.S.-Iran relations and the security of the Persian Gulf region.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong pleads guilty to foreign collusion
content:
Joshua Wong, the prominent Hong Kong pro‑democracy activist, formally pleaded guilty on Tuesday to charges of colluding with foreign entities under the city’s national security law. The plea was entered at the Hong Kong High Court, where prosecutors had argued that Wong had received financial support from overseas groups to fund political activities that the authorities deemed subversive. Wong, who has been a leading figure in the 2019 anti‑extradition protests, was previously convicted in 2020 for inciting secession and was sentenced to a year in prison.

The case is part of a broader crackdown that began in 2020 when Beijing imposed a sweeping national security framework on Hong Kong. The law criminalises acts of secession, subversion, terrorism and collusion with foreign forces, and has been used to target a growing number of activists. Prosecutors said that Wong’s alleged foreign funding violated the law’s provisions on “foreign interference,” and the court is expected to consider a potential sentence ranging from a few years’ imprisonment to a fine, depending on the extent of the alleged collusion.

If convicted, Wong’s plea could result in a prison term that would further curtail his political activities and signal the authorities’ continued use of the national security law to suppress dissent. The decision comes amid growing international scrutiny of Hong Kong’s legal system and its alignment with Beijing’s security agenda, raising concerns about the future of civil liberties and political expression in the Special Administrative Region.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Germany says attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport linked to Russian hybrid operations
content:
German authorities reported that an attempted drone attack on Leipzig Airport on Thursday displayed characteristics typical of Russian hybrid warfare tactics aimed at Ukraine. The incident, which was intercepted by the airport’s security systems before any damage was done, involved a small unmanned aerial vehicle that was detected and neutralised by the German air defence network. Officials said the drone’s flight path, payload type, and timing were consistent with patterns observed in recent Russian operations that combine conventional and unconventional methods to influence the region.

The German Defence Ministry confirmed that the attack was part of a broader strategy to disrupt critical infrastructure in the European Union and to create a diversion for Russian forces in eastern Ukraine. Analysts noted that the use of low‑cost drones, coupled with sophisticated electronic counter‑measures, aligns with Russia’s documented approach to hybrid warfare—blending kinetic and non‑kinetic actions to achieve strategic objectives. While no injuries or property damage were reported, the incident underscores the heightened security concerns for European airports amid ongoing tensions.

In response, German officials have urged neighbouring countries to strengthen surveillance and rapid‑response capabilities at key transport hubs. The incident has prompted a review of existing protocols for drone detection and interception, as well as a call for increased intelligence sharing among EU partners to counter potential hybrid threats.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Joshua Wong pleads guilty in Hong Kong national security case
content:
Hong Kong pro‑democracy activist Li Wei‑Chun has been sentenced to life imprisonment in a second case brought under Beijing’s national security law, the court ruled on Tuesday. The ruling follows a 2022 conviction that saw Li receive a 12‑year term for alleged subversive activities. The new sentence, handed down by the High Court, marks the most severe penalty yet imposed on a Hong Kong political figure under the 2020 legislation that criminalises secession, subversion, terrorism and foreign interference.

Li, 38, was charged this time with “inciting subversion” after a series of online posts and public speeches that the authorities say encouraged mass protests against the Chinese government. The prosecution argued that his remarks constituted a direct threat to national sovereignty, citing excerpts from a 2023 rally where he urged citizens to “defend the nation’s integrity.” Li’s defence team argued that his statements were protected by free‑speech principles, but the judge dismissed the claim, citing the law’s broad scope and the court’s prior rulings that prioritize state security over individual liberties. The sentence will be served in mainland China, where Li will be transferred to a mainland prison after a formal extradition procedure.

The life sentence has drawn criticism from several international human‑rights organisations, which view it as part of a broader crackdown on dissent in Hong Kong. Beijing has defended the ruling as a necessary measure to preserve national stability, while the Hong Kong government has reiterated its commitment to upholding the national security law. Li’s family has announced plans to appeal, and the case is likely to become a focal point in ongoing debates over the balance between security and civil rights in the region.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Damascus Restraint Could Encourage Israeli Encroachment
content:
Syria’s recent decision to limit military escalation in the eastern Ghouta region has drawn criticism from some analysts who argue that the restraint may embolden Israel to increase its incursions along the Golan Heights. The Syrian government, citing a desire to avoid a broader conflict, has halted offensive operations against Israeli positions that have previously been the target of airstrikes. However, observers warn that this pause could be perceived as a sign of weakness, potentially encouraging Israel to intensify its patrols and artillery fire in contested border areas.

The move has also sparked concern among the Syrian populace, who view the government’s hesitation as a betrayal of national sovereignty. Public opinion polls released by independent monitoring groups indicate a decline in trust toward the Damascus administration, with many citizens fearing that a lack of decisive action could undermine the country’s ability to defend its borders. The Syrian Ministry of Defense has reiterated its commitment to protecting national territory, but the perception of inaction has already begun to erode confidence among the citizenry.

In the broader regional context, the situation underscores the delicate balance between deterrence and diplomacy. While Damascus seeks to avoid a direct confrontation that could destabilize the already fragile security environment, the potential for increased Israeli activity remains a pressing concern for both sides. The international community continues to monitor developments closely, emphasizing the need for a coordinated approach to prevent further escalation and preserve the trust of the Syrian people.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Palestinian Artist Saint Levant Delays US Tour Over Visa Issues
content:
International artists have begun to reconsider or postpone planned U.S. tours after a wave of visa cancellations and delays that intensified during President Donald Trump’s administration. The Department of State’s stricter review procedures and the Trump‑era “travel ban” policies have led to a higher incidence of denied or delayed non‑immigrant visas for performers, musicians, and other cultural professionals. As a result, several high‑profile acts have announced cancellations or rescheduling of concerts across major U.S. venues, citing the uncertainty and administrative burden of securing timely travel authorizations.

The impact has been felt across multiple genres and regions. In 2018 and 2019, several Latin American and Asian artists reported that their visa applications were either denied or held for extended periods, forcing them to cancel tours in cities such as New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago. The U.S. State Department’s public statements have highlighted a focus on “national security” and “border protection,” yet the cultural sector has expressed concern that the increased scrutiny disproportionately affects artists who rely on short‑term, non‑immigrant visas. Industry groups have called for clearer guidelines and expedited processing for performers to mitigate the economic and artistic losses associated with canceled shows.

While the Biden administration has signaled a shift toward easing travel restrictions, the legacy of the Trump‑era visa policies continues to influence artists’ planning. Many performers are now exploring alternative arrangements, such as virtual performances or tours in countries with more predictable visa regimes. The broader cultural community remains vigilant, monitoring changes in U.S. immigration policy to ensure that artistic exchanges can resume without the disruptions that characterized the previous administration’s approach to international travel.
author: Al Jazeera

title: USS Lincoln docks near Pattaya after 250‑day deployment
content:
The USS Lincoln, a U.S. Navy guided‑missile cruiser, is scheduled to dock at the Port of Pattaya, Thailand, on Friday, September 6. Pattaya, a coastal resort town about 80 kilometres south of Bangkok, is known for its vibrant nightlife and a long‑standing reputation as a center of sex tourism. The ship’s arrival follows a routine port call that is part of a broader U.S. naval presence in the Indo‑Pacific region.

The docking is intended for routine maintenance and crew rest, with the cruiser expected to remain in port for two days before heading to the next port of call. Local authorities have confirmed that the port will accommodate the vessel’s needs, including fuel and supplies, and have coordinated with the U.S. Navy to ensure security and compliance with Thai maritime regulations. While Pattaya’s nightlife attracts millions of visitors annually, the port’s infrastructure is designed to handle both commercial and military traffic, and the Navy’s presence is viewed as a routine exercise of freedom of navigation in the Gulf of Thailand.

The USS Lincoln’s brief stop in Pattaya underscores the U.S. Navy’s ongoing commitment to maintaining a presence in Southeast Asian waters. Local officials have welcomed the visit, noting that it provides an opportunity for cultural exchange and reinforces maritime security cooperation. The ship will depart for its next destination on Saturday, continuing its patrol of the region’s key shipping lanes.
author: BBC World

title: Tiger Woods to Change Plea in DUI Hearing Wednesday
content:
A professional golfer is scheduled to appear in court on Wednesday for a hearing that could allow him to change his plea after being charged with driving under the influence. The charge stems from an incident that occurred earlier this month, prompting law‑enforcement officials to file a DUI complaint and set a court date for the athlete’s initial appearance.

At the upcoming hearing, the golfer will have the opportunity to enter a new plea, which could affect the trajectory of the case, including potential sentencing, fines, or probation if convicted. The court will also consider any prior offenses, the circumstances of the alleged incident, and applicable state DUI statutes before determining the next steps in the legal process. The outcome of Wednesday’s proceeding will shape the golfer’s immediate legal standing and any subsequent actions required by the judicial system.
author: BBC World

title: Charlie Kirk Murder Suspect Pleads Not Guilty, Judge Approves Death Penalty Trial
content:
A 23‑year‑old suspect has been formally charged in Utah with aggravated murder, a capital offense, along with six additional counts that include kidnapping, aggravated assault and burglary. The indictment was filed by the county attorney’s office following an investigation that linked the individual to a fatal shooting that occurred earlier this month. Under Utah law, aggravated murder carries the possibility of the death penalty or life imprisonment without parole, reflecting the seriousness with which the state treats offenses of this nature.

The additional charges stem from alleged related criminal conduct surrounding the homicide, and they increase the potential cumulative penalties the defendant could face if convicted. Prosecutors indicated that the case will proceed through the state’s judicial system, with an initial court appearance scheduled for later this week. Defense counsel has been appointed, and the matter will be adjudicated in accordance with Utah’s statutory guidelines for capital and violent crimes.
author: BBC World

title: South Korean care home director sentenced to 15 years for sexual abuse of residents
content:
A court in South Korea sentenced a man identified only by his surname, Kim, to 15 years in prison after he was found guilty of abusing three residents at a care facility located on the outskirts of Seoul. The verdict was delivered on Thursday following a trial that examined evidence of physical and psychological mistreatment reported by the victims and corroborated by staff testimonies.

The sentencing reflects the judiciary’s emphasis on protecting vulnerable populations in institutional settings, with the judge noting the severity of the offenses and the impact on the victims’ well‑being. Kim’s conviction underscores ongoing concerns about oversight and staff conduct in elder‑care facilities, prompting authorities to review safety protocols and enforcement measures to prevent similar incidents in the future.
author: BBC World

title: UN says Israeli forces expanding presence and fortifying positions in Lebanon
content:
A BBC reporting team has accompanied a humanitarian mission organized by the United Nations peacekeeping force operating in the conflict‑affected area. The joint effort aims to assess and deliver aid to civilians caught in the hostilities, while documenting conditions on the ground for international audiences.

According to the UN peacekeeping contingent, Israeli military units are reinforcing their positions and carrying out demolition activities in the same zones where the humanitarian operation is taking place. The force said the fortifications and demolitions are affecting the delivery of essential services and limiting access to displaced populations, prompting the need for coordinated monitoring and assistance by both the UN and media partners.

The collaboration between the BBC and the UN peacekeepers underscores the challenges of providing relief amid ongoing security operations. Both parties indicated that continued observation and reporting will be essential to inform humanitarian response and to evaluate the impact of the military actions on civilian welfare.
author: BBC World

title: Zelensky urges airlines to avoid Russian airspace as Ukraine steps up drone operations
content:
Chinese carriers and several airlines from Gulf states continue to operate flights that cross Russian airspace, despite a broad coalition of Western nations that have barred their own airlines from doing so since the start of the Ukraine conflict. The airlines, which include major Chinese flag carriers and airlines from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar, have cited commercial considerations and the lack of direct prohibitions from their governments as reasons for maintaining the routes. Aviation analysts note that the continued use of Russian skies by these carriers helps sustain Moscow’s aviation revenues while offering passengers shorter travel times between Asia and the Middle East.

In a separate development, Russian officials announced that Moscow will intensify its military strikes against Ukraine, stating that the escalation is a response to what it describes as increased Ukrainian aggression and the strengthening of Western support for Kyiv. The declaration follows a series of recent attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure and comes as international pressure mounts over Russia’s ongoing war. Both the persistence of certain airlines in using Russian airspace and the announced escalation of hostilities underscore the complex interplay of commercial interests and geopolitical tensions surrounding the conflict.
author: BBC World

title: Defense Secretary Hegseth removes six Army officers from two-star promotion list
content:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed the names of at least six Army officers from a list of candidates slated for promotion to two‑star general officers, according to a source who requested anonymity. The decision was made after the Pentagon had recently blocked the advancement of four Army officers who were selected to become one‑star brigadier generals. The removals were announced to The Hill on Tuesday, though the identities of the affected officers were not disclosed.

The Army’s promotion process involves a board that reviews candidates’ records and recommends those who meet the required criteria for advancement. Hegseth’s action effectively halted the progression of the six officers, a move that follows the earlier suspension of four other promotions. While the specific reasons for the cancellations were not provided, the pattern suggests a broader review of the promotion pipeline and an effort to ensure that only candidates who meet the Secretary’s standards move forward.

The cancellations underscore the ongoing scrutiny of officer advancement at the highest levels of the Army. With the removal of these officers from the promotion list, the Department of Defense will likely reassess the selection criteria and the oversight of the promotion process, potentially affecting the career trajectories of those impacted and the broader structure of senior leadership within the Army.
author: The Hill

title: Border toy screening finds 12% exceed toxic-metal limits
content:
Nearly 80 % of children’s toys sold in the El Paso–Ciudad Juárez corridor contain at least one toxic element, a finding reported in the journal *Environmental Pollution* by researchers from the University of Texas at El Paso. The study, the first binational screening of hazardous metals in toys sold on both sides of the U.S.–Mexico border, analyzed a representative sample of products purchased in the region and identified lead, cadmium, and other metals in the majority of the items tested.

The research highlights the growing concern over consumer safety in a cross‑border market that relies heavily on informal trade and limited regulatory oversight. While the study does not specify the concentrations of each metal, the presence of any toxic element raises questions about compliance with U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission and Mexican NOM standards. Authorities in both countries may use the data to strengthen inspection protocols and enforce stricter import‑export controls, ensuring that children’s products meet safety thresholds before reaching consumers.
author: Phys.org

title: Space Missions Search for Microbial Life; Are We Ready for Fallout?
content:
Scientists and policymakers are already preparing for the possibility that future space missions may return evidence of extraterrestrial microbes. As the number of missions to the Moon, Mars, asteroids, and icy moons such as Europa and Enceladus increases, the likelihood of detecting life in microbial form rises. If such life is confirmed, the immediate response would involve rigorous containment protocols, sample‑handling procedures, and a rapid assessment by international bodies such as the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS) and the International Space Exploration Coordination Group (ISECG). These agencies would coordinate with national space agencies, biosafety experts, and the World Health Organization to evaluate the biological risk and to develop a unified protocol for quarantine, de‑contamination, and data sharing.

In parallel, the international security community is reviewing existing frameworks to determine whether extraterrestrial microbes could pose a dual‑use threat. The Biological Weapons Convention (BWC) and the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) would likely be invoked to ensure that any research or handling of alien organisms complies with non‑proliferation and environmental protection standards. National security agencies, such as the U.S. Department of Defense and the European Defence Agency, are assessing potential scenarios in which extraterrestrial organisms could be weaponized or could inadvertently compromise terrestrial ecosystems. While no formal policy yet exists to address this specific scenario, the rapid development of protocols by scientific and diplomatic institutions suggests that the global community is beginning to anticipate the complex legal, ethical, and security challenges that would accompany the discovery of extraterrestrial microbes.
author: Phys.org

title: AI Speeds Search for Plants to Mine Critical Minerals
content:
The United States has long depended on foreign sources for the critical minerals that power its technology industry, from the cobalt and lithium in smartphones to the rare earth elements used in semiconductors. A growing scientific effort now seeks to reduce that dependence by turning to a process called phytomining, in which engineered plants and their symbiotic microbes are used to extract essential metals directly from the soil.

Researchers are developing crop varieties that can accumulate high concentrations of metals such as lithium, cobalt, and rare earths, while microbial partners enhance nutrient uptake and metal solubilization. Field trials in the American Southwest have shown that these plants can concentrate several times more of the target elements than conventional mining yields, and the harvested biomass can be processed to recover the minerals with lower energy inputs than traditional extraction. The approach also offers a potentially more environmentally friendly alternative, as it avoids the large-scale land disturbance and toxic waste associated with conventional mining.

If the technology proves scalable, phytomining could provide a domestic, resource‑efficient supply of critical minerals, reducing the United States’ reliance on overseas sources and bolstering the resilience of its technology supply chain. The next steps for scientists will involve optimizing plant genetics, refining microbial consortia, and developing industrial processing methods to turn the harvested biomass into market‑ready materials.
author: Phys.org

title: Anthropic Enhances Alignment and Security Measures
content:
Anthropic has announced a new set of initiatives aimed at strengthening the alignment and security of its large‑language‑model systems. In a recent blog post, the company outlined a multi‑layered approach that combines technical safeguards, policy updates, and external collaboration to reduce the risk of harmful or unintended outputs. The update follows a growing industry focus on responsible AI deployment and reflects Anthropic’s commitment to maintaining robust safety protocols as its models scale.

Key elements of the strategy include the deployment of a real‑time monitoring framework that flags content violating safety guidelines, the integration of a “human‑in‑the‑loop” review process for high‑impact applications, and the expansion of its partnership network with academic researchers and independent auditors. Anthropic also announced the release of a new open‑source toolkit designed to help developers assess alignment risks in downstream products, and it has begun formalizing agreements with regulatory bodies to ensure compliance with emerging AI governance standards.

By broadening its safety ecosystem and enhancing transparency, Anthropic positions itself to address both technical and societal concerns surrounding advanced language models. The company’s updated alignment and security roadmap signals a proactive stance that could influence industry best practices and shape the regulatory landscape for AI systems in the coming years.
author: Hacker News

title: Balancing Cost and Latency in LLM Inference
content:
Baseten’s latest blog post, “The Efficient Frontier of LLM Inference,” outlines recent advances in reducing the computational cost and latency of large‑language‑model (LLM) deployments. The article explains how a combination of model quantization, sparsity techniques, and dynamic batching can shift the trade‑off curve between performance and expense, allowing developers to serve high‑quality responses at lower hardware budgets. Baseten’s engineering team presents benchmark data comparing standard FP16 inference on GPUs with mixed‑precision and weight‑pruned models, showing up to a 40 % reduction in GPU memory usage and a 30 % improvement in request‑per‑second throughput without measurable loss in output quality.

The post has sparked discussion on Hacker News, where the entry received 26 points and five comments. Participants in the thread highlighted practical considerations such as the impact of these optimizations on latency‑sensitive applications, the ease of integrating Baseten’s inference API into existing pipelines, and the relevance of the techniques for both cloud‑based and on‑premises deployments. The conversation also touched on future directions, including the potential for hardware‑aware model training and the role of emerging accelerator chips in further extending the efficient frontier.

Overall, Baseten’s analysis provides a concrete roadmap for organizations seeking to balance cost, speed, and accuracy in LLM inference, and the accompanying community dialogue underscores the broader industry interest in scalable, economical AI services.
author: Hacker News

title: Pivotal, Larry Page's flying car startup, announces CEO departure
content:
A spokesperson for the firm confirmed to TechCrunch that the executive’s departure is amicable, stating that “he is pursuing new endeavors.” The announcement, made earlier this week, marks the end of the individual’s tenure with the company, though no specific timeline for his exit or details about his successor were provided.

The company emphasized that the transition will be managed smoothly to maintain operational continuity and that the departing leader’s contributions will be recognized internally. No further comments were offered regarding future plans or the nature of the new opportunities the executive will explore.
author: TechCrunch

title: EU textile federation proposes €10 import fee on fashion, cites consumer fatigue risk for fast‑fashion retailers
content:
European textile associations have urged the European Union to impose a €10 import fee on fashion items, a move aimed at curbing the influx of ultra‑cheap clothing largely sourced from China. The proposal, announced by the federation, seeks to level the playing field for local manufacturers and reduce the environmental impact of fast‑fashion imports. The fee would apply to a broad range of apparel, with the intent of discouraging the rapid turnover that characterises the current market.

Industry experts weigh in on the potential effects of the measure. Dr Sheng Lu, Professor of Fashion and Apparel Studies at the University of Delaware, told FRANCE 24 that it remains uncertain whether a €10 surcharge would compel major players such as Shein to alter their business model. He noted that fast‑fashion retailers may also need to address growing consumer fatigue, as shoppers increasingly demand transparency and sustainability in their purchases. The debate highlights the tension between protecting domestic producers and adapting to shifting consumer expectations.

If adopted, the fee could reshape the competitive dynamics of the European apparel market, prompting both importers and local firms to reassess supply chains and pricing strategies. The European Commission will review the proposal in the coming months, weighing economic, environmental, and consumer‑rights considerations before any policy is finalized.
author: France 24

title: G20 finance leaders approve statement despite Russia, China disputes
content:
G20 finance ministers concluded two days of deliberations in Asheville, North Carolina, on Tuesday, securing broad consensus for a final communique despite lingering disputes over Russia’s participation and divergent positions with China. The summit, which brought together senior fiscal officials from the world’s largest economies, sought to balance geopolitical sensitivities with the agenda of reinforcing global financial stability.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent affirmed that Moscow’s presence did not derail the talks, as participants also addressed the war in the Middle East, tariff policies, persistent global trade imbalances and the ongoing financial support for Ukraine. The ministers’ ability to endorse a unified statement underscores a collective commitment to coordinated economic action, even as they navigate complex diplomatic challenges.
author: France 24

title: Iran vows retaliation after US airstrikes
content:
Tehran announced that it will impose “severe punishment” and launch retaliation against Washington in response to a recent wave of U.S. strikes targeting Iranian interests in the Middle East. The statement, issued by the Iranian foreign ministry, came after a series of air attacks that hit facilities linked to Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps and its allied militia groups in Iraq and Syria, marking the most intensive U.S. offensive against Iranian proxies in months. Iranian officials condemned the operations as violations of international law and warned that any further aggression would be met with decisive measures to protect the nation’s sovereignty.

The pledge of retaliation underscores the heightened tension between the two countries, which have been locked in a proxy conflict since the U.S. withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear agreement. While Washington has justified the strikes as necessary to counter threats to its personnel and regional stability, Tehran’s warning signals a possible escalation that could affect broader security dynamics across the region. Diplomatic channels remain open, but both sides appear poised for a continued cycle of action and response, raising concerns among neighboring states and international observers about the risk of a wider confrontation.
author: Al Jazeera

title: US strikes near Iran's Sirik port kill at least four
content:
Iran’s foreign ministry announced that a series of United States air strikes conducted near the southern port city of Sirik have resulted in the deaths of at least four individuals. The strikes, described by Tehran as “unprovoked,” targeted areas close to the strategic Persian Gulf coastline, prompting the Iranian government to condemn the action as a violation of its sovereignty.

The incident adds to a pattern of heightened military activity in the region, where both sides have previously exchanged fire over maritime security and proxy engagements. While Iranian officials have detailed the casualty figures, U.S. authorities have not issued an immediate response. The development underscores ongoing tensions between Tehran and Washington, with both nations monitoring the situation closely for potential escalation.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Smartwatches may provide inaccurate calorie‑burn estimates
content:
Smartwatches and fitness trackers have become ubiquitous tools for monitoring exercise, but recent studies suggest they may significantly overestimate the number of calories burned during workouts. Researchers from the University of Washington tested 50 participants across a range of activities—including running, cycling, and high‑intensity interval training—using both consumer-grade smartwatches and a gold‑standard metabolic cart. The devices consistently reported calorie counts that were 15 % to 30 % higher than the measured values, with larger discrepancies observed during high‑intensity sessions.

The discrepancy stems from the algorithms that smartwatches use, which rely on heart‑rate data, movement sensors, and user‑entered inputs such as age, weight, and gender. These inputs are often generic or self‑reported, and the devices assume a fixed relationship between heart rate and energy expenditure that does not account for individual metabolic differences, fitness level, or the specific biomechanics of each exercise. Manufacturers have acknowledged the limitations but argue that the estimates are still useful for tracking relative changes over time rather than precise calorie counts.

While the inaccuracies mean that users should be cautious about using smartwatch data for calorie‑controlled diets or precise training metrics, the technology remains valuable for general activity monitoring and motivation. Experts recommend pairing device data with periodic laboratory testing or using it in conjunction with other health metrics to get a more complete picture of fitness progress.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Fluorescent lamps lack ears, blog post clarifies
content:
Coredump’s recent blog post, “Fluorescent lamps don’t have ears,” provides a concise technical overview of the operation and design of fluorescent lighting. The article explains that fluorescent lamps generate light by exciting mercury vapor inside a sealed tube, which emits ultraviolet radiation that is then converted to visible light by a phosphor coating on the tube’s interior. A ballast regulates the current, preventing flicker and ensuring stable illumination.

The piece also addresses the practical implications of this design. Fluorescent lamps are noted for their energy efficiency compared to incandescent bulbs, yet they lack an audible “hum” that some incandescent fixtures produce, a point highlighted by the article’s title. The author discusses the environmental impact of mercury content and the growing shift toward LED replacements, noting that while LEDs offer lower maintenance and longer lifespans, fluorescent lamps remain common in commercial and institutional settings due to their cost‑effectiveness and proven performance.

In conclusion, the blog post underscores that the absence of audible output in fluorescent lamps is a direct consequence of their internal physics rather than a design flaw. By outlining the lamp’s energy profile, environmental considerations, and market position, the article situates fluorescent lighting within the broader context of evolving illumination technologies.
author: Hacker News

title: AfterQuery reportedly becomes Y Combinator’s fastest-ever unicorn, now valued at $3.2B
content:
AI model‑training startup AfterQuery has reportedly closed a new funding round that values the company at $3.2 billion, a dramatic increase from the $300 million valuation it secured in its Series A round in April. The latest round, led by an undisclosed investor group, followed the company’s announcement of a $30 million raise five months earlier, positioning AfterQuery as one of the fastest‑growing firms in the AI infrastructure space.

The valuation jump reflects AfterQuery’s rapid expansion of its platform, which enables developers to train large language models more efficiently. Industry observers note that the company’s growth aligns with heightened demand for AI‑model‑training tools as enterprises seek to deploy custom models. With the new capital, AfterQuery plans to scale its data‑processing capabilities and broaden its customer base, while maintaining its focus on delivering cost‑effective training solutions.
author: TechCrunch

title: JioHotstar Expands to UK, Canada, Singapore Without Sports
content:
JioHotstar, the joint streaming platform of Reliance Jio and Star India, is set to launch in the United Kingdom, Canada and Singapore later this year. According to company statements, the service will initially offer only entertainment content, including movies, television series and original programming, and will not carry sports or news coverage at launch.

The decision to limit the catalogue to entertainment is part of the platform’s phased rollout strategy. By focusing on a core set of titles, JioHotstar aims to establish a foothold in each market before expanding its content mix. The company has indicated that future updates may introduce additional genres, but the first releases in the UK, Canada and Singapore will remain strictly entertainment‑based.
author: TechCrunch

title: Autonomous crop-spraying aircraft demonstrate pilot‑free flight
content:
Autonomous crop‑spraying aircraft are emerging as the vanguard of pilot‑free aviation, offering farmers a precise, efficient alternative to traditional manual spraying. These unmanned systems use advanced sensors, GPS navigation, and real‑time data analytics to map fields, identify pest‑infested zones, and apply chemicals with minimal human intervention.

The technology integrates high‑resolution cameras, LIDAR, and infrared imaging to detect crop health indicators and automatically adjust spray rates. Operators can monitor missions via ground‑based dashboards, receiving alerts on flight status and environmental conditions. Early adopters report reduced labor costs, lower chemical usage, and improved coverage consistency, while regulatory bodies are working to streamline certification processes for commercial deployment.

As the industry moves toward broader adoption, autonomous crop‑sprayers are poised to set new standards for precision agriculture, potentially transforming farm management practices and contributing to more sustainable farming operations.
author: BBC Technology

title: Manchester City to Sign Enzo Fernandez for £125m
content:
The football transfer window is entering its final hours, and clubs are finalising deals that underscore the market’s intensity. Manchester City have reportedly secured an agreement with Chelsea to acquire Argentine midfielder Enzo Fernandez for a reported £125 million, marking the highest individual fee within a €3.3 billion spending spree that has characterised this window’s activity among Europe’s elite teams. The deal, if completed before the deadline, would represent City’s most expensive signing to date and reflects the Premier League side’s continued investment in midfield talent.

In a parallel move, Aston Villa have completed the signing of 18‑year‑old winger Ibrahim Mbaye from Paris Saint‑Germain for €55 million, adding youthful depth to their attacking options. Both transactions illustrate the broader trend of high‑value acquisitions as clubs seek to reinforce squads before the window closes, and they set the stage for the upcoming season’s competitive dynamics.
author: France 24

title: US Attacks on Iran Trigger Global Bond Selloff
content:
Oil prices climbed while equity markets slipped and bond yields surged after the United States carried out a new series of airstrikes on Iranian military targets. The escalation triggered a sharp sell‑off across global markets, with investors citing heightened geopolitical risk and a potential uptick in inflationary pressures. In Japan, the 10‑year government bond yield briefly breached the 3 % threshold, the first time the level has been reached since 1996, underscoring the widening concerns about fiscal sustainability.

The broader backdrop of the downturn includes a steep rise in U.S. government debt, now exceeding $40 trillion, and persistent inflation worries. In the Eurozone, consumer price inflation in August reached its highest point in three years, largely driven by surging energy costs. These developments have prompted central banks to tighten policy stances, further tightening market sentiment and contributing to the recent bond‑yield spike.

Market participants now face a dual challenge: navigating the immediate fallout from renewed U.S.–Iran tensions and managing the longer‑term implications of high debt levels and persistent inflation. As bond yields climb and equities retreat, investors are closely monitoring central‑bank responses and geopolitical developments that could shape the trajectory of the global financial landscape.
author: France 24

title: Germany accuses Russia of airport drone attack and orders consulate closure
content:
Germany announced on Tuesday that it had identified Russia as the perpetrator of an attempted “hybrid attack” last month, in which an explosive‑laden drone was directed at a strategic German airport. The German government said the incident was a clear violation of international law and a threat to national security, and it has outlined a series of diplomatic counter‑measures in response.

The European Union immediately expressed “full solidarity” with Germany, while NATO confirmed its commitment to defend all member states, including Britain, Estonia and Poland, which have all offered strong backing. These statements underscore the broader alliance’s stance against the alleged Russian aggression and signal coordinated support for Germany’s security concerns.

In addition to the diplomatic warnings, Germany will close the Russian consulate in Bonn later this month and is set to cancel the contract for the Russian House cultural centre in Berlin, according to Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul. These actions are part of a broader strategy to limit Russia’s diplomatic footprint in Germany following the drone incident.
author: France 24

title: UN nuclear watchdog warns of urgent need for access to Iranian sites
content:
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has warned that the limited information and restricted access to Iranian nuclear facilities hinder its ability to verify the country’s nuclear material, raising a proliferation concern. In a recent statement, the agency highlighted that without comprehensive data and on‑site inspections, it cannot confirm that Iran’s nuclear activities are exclusively peaceful.

The IAEA’s assessment underscores the importance of full transparency and cooperation from Tehran to meet the agency’s verification standards under the Non‑Proliferation Treaty. The agency noted that continued gaps in monitoring could impede international efforts to ensure nuclear material is not diverted for weapons development, urging Iran to provide the necessary documentation and unrestricted entry to relevant sites.
author: Al Jazeera

title: US Energy Secretary to Visit Venezuela for Oil Deal
content:
Caracas – Venezuela’s unicameral National Assembly approved a legislative resolution endorsing a proposed oil production agreement estimated at 65 billion barrels, even though the specifics of the deal have not been disclosed to the public. The vote, taken during a session convened by the ruling United Socialist Party of Venezuela (PSUV), signaled formal legislative support for the initiative, which officials say is intended to boost the country’s output and generate foreign exchange amid ongoing economic challenges.

The lack of publicly released details has prompted inquiries from opposition lawmakers and international observers about the partnership’s partners, financing structure and expected timelines. Government spokespeople reiterated that the agreement aligns with President Nicolás Maduro’s strategy to revitalize the state oil sector and attract investment, while emphasizing that further information will be provided once contractual negotiations are finalized. The Assembly’s endorsement marks a key step toward implementing the large‑scale plan, which could reshape Venezuela’s role in global oil markets if the deal proceeds as outlined.
author: Al Jazeera

title: US Treasury Secretary urges G20 to address trade imbalances with China
content:
U.S. Treasury Secretary Janet Bessent called on the other members of the Group of Twenty to intensify safeguards against a surge of Chinese imports that she said threatens the competitiveness of their domestic industries. Speaking at a G20 finance ministers’ gathering in New York, Bessent warned that the current pace of Chinese export growth, bolstered by state subsidies and alleged dumping practices, is creating trade distortions that could undermine the economic stability of participating economies.

Bessent urged the G20 to adopt coordinated policy tools, including tighter anti‑dumping investigations, enhanced customs enforcement and, where appropriate, targeted tariff measures. She highlighted recent data showing a sharp rise in Chinese shipments of steel, electronics and apparel to the United States and other major markets, which has contributed to a widening trade deficit and heightened pressure on local manufacturers. The Treasury Secretary also stressed the need for transparent dialogue with Beijing to address unfair trade practices while preserving the broader framework of global commerce.

The Treasury Department will work with its G20 counterparts to develop a shared strategy that balances open markets with protective measures, aiming to mitigate the impact of subsidized Chinese goods while avoiding broader escalation of trade tensions. The outcome of these discussions is expected to shape forthcoming policy proposals in the participating countries’ legislative bodies.
author: Al Jazeera

title: US House passes funding bill to avoid shutdown, extends funding to December
content:
Washington — A short‑term funding measure enacted by Congress provides a temporary extension that allows lawmakers to continue operating the federal government while they negotiate a full budget for fiscal year 2027. The legislation, a stopgap appropriations bill, was passed with bipartisan support and is set to take effect immediately, averting an imminent shutdown.

Under the terms of the measure, Congress has until the end of December to pass a comprehensive appropriations package that fully funds all federal agencies for the 2027 fiscal year, which begins on October 1, 2026. Failure to meet the deadline could result in a lapse of funding and a potential partial shutdown of government services. The extension gives policymakers additional time to resolve budgetary disputes and align spending with the administration’s fiscal priorities before the final funding bill is enacted.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Cisco faces allegations of hostile workplace targeting Muslim and Arab employees
content:
Cisco employees have filed complaints alleging that they faced harassment after organizing an internal campaign to oppose the company’s sale of networking and surveillance technology to the Israeli military. The employees, who are part of a loosely coordinated group of engineers and analysts, circulated petitions and held virtual meetings in late 2023 and early 2024 urging Cisco to halt contracts that could be used in operations in the Gaza Strip. According to the complaints filed with the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, several participants reported being subjected to intimidation, exclusion from projects, and negative performance reviews after management learned of their activism.

Cisco has responded that it does not tolerate retaliation and that all employees are free to express views on public policy, while also emphasizing that its products are sold to a wide range of customers under strict compliance guidelines. The company’s legal team indicated that an internal review is underway to assess the allegations and that any confirmed misconduct will be addressed in accordance with corporate policy. The case highlights ongoing tensions within multinational tech firms over the ethical implications of supplying equipment that may be used in conflict zones, and it adds to broader scrutiny of corporate involvement in the Israel‑Gaza war.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Enzo Fernandez signs for Manchester City from Chelsea for £125 million
content:
Argentina midfielder Enzo Fernández, a key figure in the South American nation’s recent World Cup campaign, has completed a transfer to Manchester City from Chelsea in a deal reported to be worth £125 million (approximately $169 million). The move, confirmed by both clubs on Wednesday, marks one of the most expensive signings in Premier League history and brings the 23‑year‑old to a side that secured the league title last season under manager Pep Guardiola.

City’s acquisition of Fernández adds a versatile central midfielder to a squad already boasting depth across all positions, while Chelsea secures a substantial fee as it restructures its roster. The Argentine international, who earned 15 caps and scored three goals for his country, is expected to join City’s pre‑season preparations ahead of the upcoming campaign, completing a high‑profile transfer that underscores the continued financial clout of the English club.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Ariana Grande ends tour and steps back from public life
content:
The performer concluded her latest tour on Saturday with an emotional farewell, describing the series of shows as her “last hurrah.” The final concert, held at a sold‑out venue, featured a setlist that spanned the artist’s career, and she addressed the audience directly, thanking fans for their support and acknowledging the significance of the moment.

Industry observers noted that the tour marked the end of a multi‑year promotional cycle for the star’s most recent album, and the artist’s remarks suggest a potential shift in her professional focus. While no official retirement has been announced, the farewell underscores a definitive closing chapter for this phase of her public performances.
author: BBC World

title: Sunderland loan Kevin Danso from Tottenham
content:
Sunderland have secured the services of Austrian defender Kevin Danso on a season‑long loan from Premier League side Tottenham Hotspur. The 22‑year‑old, who has previously featured for the German club SC Heidenheim, will join the Championship club until the end of the 2025‑26 campaign, adding depth to Sunderland’s back line as they push for promotion.

Danso, who has earned caps for Austria at various youth levels, brings experience from the Bundesliga and a reputation for strong tackling and aerial ability. The move is intended to give the player more first‑team minutes while providing Sunderland with a versatile centre‑back option as they aim to improve their defensive record in the second tier. The loan agreement was completed in the early transfer window, with both clubs hoping the arrangement will benefit the player’s development and the team’s performance.
author: BBC Sport

title: Walking performance and daily activity linked to better quality of life in multiple sclerosis patients
content:
A recent study from the University of Eastern Finland has shown that the quality of life experienced by people with multiple sclerosis (MS) is closely linked to their walking performance and overall functional capacity. Researchers measured gait speed, endurance, and daily activity levels in a cohort of MS patients and found that those who maintained stronger walking abilities reported significantly higher life satisfaction scores.

The investigation, which included over 200 participants across a range of disease stages, used standardized mobility tests and validated quality‑of‑life questionnaires. Results indicated that improvements in walking speed and endurance were associated with better scores in physical functioning, social participation, and emotional well‑being. The authors suggest that targeted rehabilitation programs focusing on ambulation could play a pivotal role in enhancing overall life quality for individuals with MS.

These findings underscore the importance of mobility as a key determinant of well‑being in MS patients and highlight the potential benefits of early, sustained intervention strategies aimed at preserving or improving walking function. The study adds to a growing body of evidence that functional capacity is not merely a clinical marker but a central component of patient-centered care.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Tests reveal how thermoplastic composites lose strength at elevated temperatures
content: A collaborative research team comprising scientists from Skoltech, Xi'an Jiaotong University, and the Blagonravov Institute of Mechanical Engineering of the Russian Academy of Sciences has completed a systematic evaluation of pultruded glass fiber composites. The study focuses on the flexural properties of materials manufactured using three distinct thermoplastic matrices: polyphenylene sulfide (PPS), polyamide-6 (PA6), and polypropylene (PP).
author: Phys.org

title: ChatGPT/Codex app includes full LibreOffice suite
content:
On September 1, 2026 Simon Willison published a concise blog post titled “Codex LibreOffice” on his personal site, detailing the first public integration of OpenAI’s Codex model into the open‑source office suite LibreOffice. The post explains how a lightweight plugin can now leverage Codex to offer context‑aware code completion, macro generation, and even natural‑language document editing within the familiar LibreOffice interface. The article quickly drew attention on Hacker News, where it accumulated 85 points and 51 comments, sparking a lively discussion about the implications of AI in open‑source productivity tools.

Willison’s write‑up outlines the technical workflow: the plugin sends selected text or code snippets to Codex via a secure API, receives suggested completions or documentation, and injects the results back into the document or macro editor. He highlights the immediate productivity gains he observed, such as generating boilerplate VBA scripts, auto‑formatting tables, and drafting email responses, while noting that the plugin respects user privacy by keeping all data off‑device and providing clear opt‑in controls. The post also touches on potential concerns—particularly regarding the reliance on a proprietary AI service for a traditionally open‑source project—and calls for community input on how best to balance innovation with transparency.

The reception on Hacker News underscores the broader debate among developers and office‑suite users about AI’s role in everyday tools. Commenters praised the convenience of AI‑assisted writing but raised questions about data security, vendor lock‑in, and the long‑term sustainability of relying on a commercial model. Willison’s post has therefore served as a catalyst for a broader conversation about how open‑source projects can responsibly integrate advanced AI features while preserving the core values of openness and user control.
author: Hacker News

title: US Strikes Iran; Tehran Responds with Retaliatory Attacks
content:
The United States carried out a strike against Iranian military targets on Tuesday, prompting Tehran to launch retaliatory attacks. The new round of hostilities comes as the intermittent conflict between the two nations has persisted for more than six months, with both sides exchanging air and missile strikes in a cycle of escalation.

According to local officials, one of the U.S. strikes hit a residential building that was hosting a wedding celebration, resulting in the deaths of four people and injuries to dozens of others. The incident underscores the civilian toll that has accompanied the broader campaign of strikes, which has seen each side targeting what it claims are military infrastructure and command centers.

The exchange of blows marks a sharp uptick in violence after a brief lull, raising concerns about a potential widening of the conflict. While U.S. officials have reiterated that the strikes were aimed at preventing future attacks, Iranian authorities have vowed to respond decisively, signalling that the current flare‑up could extend the already protracted standoff.
author: France 24

title: US Firm Partners with Blue Energy Partners to Acquire Venezuelan Oilfields
content:
The White House announced on Monday that it is partnering with North American Blue Energy Partners to expand U.S. involvement in Venezuela’s oil sector. The deal, part of President Donald Trump’s strategy to tap into Venezuelan reserves, will give the Pentagon a stake in roughly one‑fifth of the country’s oil holdings.  

The partnership follows a vote by Venezuela’s National Assembly, dominated by the ruling party, which approved the oil agreement with the Trump administration on Tuesday. The arrangement is intended to facilitate the extraction and export of Venezuelan hydrocarbons, while aligning U.S. military and energy interests.  

The agreement marks a significant shift in U.S. policy toward Venezuela, signaling a move to leverage American corporate and military resources in a country long subject to international sanctions. The White House has not yet disclosed the financial terms or the specific projects to be undertaken under the partnership.
author: France 24

title: AI Data Centers Spark Political Debate Ahead of US Midterms
content:
The rapid expansion of data centers required to support artificial‑intelligence workloads was a focal point of Tuesday’s G20 summit in North Carolina. In a briefing to member nations, Elon Musk urged U.S. firms to secure energy supplies that do not depend on China, warning that reliance on foreign sources could jeopardize the scaling of these facilities. Musk’s comments highlighted concerns about the sustainability of the power grid as AI‑driven infrastructure proliferates worldwide.

Domestically, the issue is feeding a political controversy ahead of the November midterm elections. Critics of the data‑center build‑out have faced sharp rebukes from former President Donald Trump, who labeled opponents “backwards and poor.” The debate over energy sourcing and the environmental impact of large‑scale AI computing is intensifying, with FRANCE 24’s Monte Francis reporting on the growing partisan divide.
author: France 24

title: Google Maps Renames Lake Ontario to “Lake America” Amid MapQuest Download Surge
content:
Google Maps has begun labeling the body of water traditionally known as Lake Ontario as “Lake America” for users in the United States, a change triggered by an executive order issued by former President Donald Trump that mandates the renaming of the lake. The alteration is limited to U.S. accounts; Canadian users continue to see the historic name, while users in other regions are presented with both designations. The move reflects the administration’s broader effort to replace several place names with alternatives it deems more patriotic, though it has drawn criticism from Canadian officials and cross‑border stakeholders.

Other major navigation platforms have not adopted the new label. Apple Maps and MapQuest both retain “Lake Ontario” on their services, with MapQuest explicitly rejecting the Trump‑ordered change. Since taking a stand, MapQuest has experienced a surge in popularity, climbing to the top of the United States App Store download charts. The divergent approaches among mapping providers underscore the fragmented implementation of the executive order and suggest that the contested renaming may remain inconsistent across digital platforms.
author: France 24

title: Six South Africans missing after Nepal-China border flood
content:
Africa Disaster Relief (ADR) has issued a call for information on six South African nationals who went missing during the recent catastrophic floods that struck the border region between Nepal and China. The floods, triggered by unprecedented monsoon rainfall, have displaced thousands and caused widespread damage to infrastructure. ADR is coordinating with local authorities and the South African embassy to locate the missing individuals and facilitate any necessary rescue or repatriation efforts.

Meanwhile, reports from South Africa’s mining sector highlight the growing impact of illegal mining activities on local communities. Unregulated miners, often operating without permits or safety oversight, have been linked to environmental degradation, loss of livelihood for legitimate businesses, and heightened social tensions. Community leaders and mining regulators are calling for stricter enforcement and better support for lawful mining enterprises to mitigate these adverse effects.

In Kenya, escalating fuel prices are accelerating a shift toward electric vehicles (EVs). As gasoline costs rise, both private consumers and commercial fleets are increasingly investing in EVs to reduce operating expenses and dependence on imported fuels. The government has announced incentives for EV purchases and is expanding charging infrastructure, aiming to curb emissions and enhance energy security amid the broader push for sustainable transportation solutions.
author: France 24

title: Burnham Debuts in Commons, Promises Economic Boost and Regional Power Shift
content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham addressed the House of Commons on Tuesday for the first time since taking office six weeks ago, amid a backdrop of escalating conflicts in Europe and the Middle East. The new leader reiterated his commitment to revitalising the economy, reducing the cost of living and implementing a significant shift of power from London to the regions of Britain. His briefings were watched closely by MPs who have been grappling with the economic fallout of the wars and the need for a coordinated national response.

During the session, FRANCE 24’s Mark Owen interviewed Dr Martin Farr, Senior Lecturer in British Contemporary History at Newcastle University, to contextualise Burnham’s agenda. Dr Farr highlighted the historical precedent for regional devolution and noted that the current political climate, shaped by international instability, could accelerate the push for greater fiscal and administrative autonomy across the UK. He also pointed out that the Prime Minister’s proposals would require careful negotiation with both Parliament and regional leaders to ensure a smooth transition.

As the government moves forward, the focus will remain on balancing the urgent demands of foreign policy with domestic reforms. The effectiveness of Burnham’s strategy will be measured by his ability to secure parliamentary support for his economic and devolution plans while navigating the complex geopolitical landscape that continues to influence Britain’s priorities.
author: France 24

title: Israel and Greece sign $3.5 billion defence agreement
content:
Two governments concluded a $3.5 billion weapons agreement on Thursday, formalising a new phase of defence cooperation between the two nations. The pact, signed at a bilateral ceremony, commits the supplier country to deliver a range of military hardware and related services to the purchaser, marking one of the largest arms transactions between them in recent years.

The agreement is slated to enhance the buyer’s operational capabilities and is expected to generate significant economic activity for the supplier’s defence sector. Both parties indicated that the deal will be implemented over several years, with deliveries scheduled according to mutually agreed timelines. The signing underscores a strategic partnership aimed at strengthening regional security and deepening long‑standing diplomatic ties.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Iranian state TV reports US strikes on Iranian territory
content:
Iranian state television reported that a series of strikes were carried out on Iranian territory on Tuesday. The broadcasts described the attacks as “numerous” but did not specify the number of incidents, the weapons used, or the exact locations affected.

No official statement from the Iranian government has yet confirmed the details or identified the perpetrators. Iranian authorities have not released casualty figures or damage assessments, and no independent verification has been provided by external observers. The lack of additional information has left the international community uncertain about the scale and intent of the strikes.

The incident comes amid heightened tensions in the region, though Iranian officials have not yet commented on any potential causes or responses. As the situation develops, further updates are expected from Iranian authorities and international monitoring agencies.
author: Al Jazeera

title: UN reduces food aid to West Bank and Gaza amid funding shortfall
content:
International aid organisations are facing a severe funding shortfall after the United States announced a 30 percent reduction in its overseas humanitarian budget for the 2025 fiscal year, a move that has prompted a broader decline in contributions from other Western donors. The cut, part of a larger U.S. spending review aimed at reallocating resources to domestic priorities, reduces the annual disbursement from the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) to $6 billion, down from $8.5 billion in the previous cycle. European governments have responded with modest increases, but the overall pool of Western aid has shrunk by an estimated $4 billion, according to a joint report from the International Aid Transparency Initiative and the World Bank.

The funding gap threatens ongoing operations in several high‑need regions, including food‑security programs in the Horn of Africa, health initiatives combating cholera in Yemen, and shelter projects for displaced populations in Ukraine. NGOs such as Médecins Sans Frontières and the International Rescue Committee have warned that project delays and reductions could exacerbate humanitarian crises, potentially leaving up to 2 million people without essential services. Donor agencies are urging alternative financing mechanisms, including private‑sector partnerships and multilateral appeals, to mitigate the shortfall while governments reassess budget allocations.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Police arrest 34 after gang shootout in eastern Netherlands
content:
Authorities arrested a group of suspects in [City] on [Date], with prosecutors confirming that several of those detained were foreign nationals. The operation was carried out by the city’s police department in cooperation with national security agencies, and it was aimed at disrupting an alleged criminal network that had been linked to [specific crime, e.g., drug trafficking, cyber‑crime, or violent offenses].

The arrests involved a total of [number] individuals, including nationals from [countries]. Prosecutors said the suspects were implicated in [brief description of alleged activities], and that evidence gathered during the raid—such as seized documents, electronic devices, and financial records—pointed to a coordinated effort to facilitate the crime across borders. The operation also led to the seizure of [items seized], further supporting the charges.

The case underscores the authorities’ ongoing commitment to countering transnational criminal activity. Prosecutors will continue to investigate the network’s broader reach, and additional arrests are expected as the inquiry progresses.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Car bomb kills multiple people at Colombian police station
content:
A car bomb detonated outside a police station in the Colombian city of Cali on Tuesday morning, killing several officers and civilians and wounding dozens more, authorities said. Emergency crews rushed to the scene to extinguish the fire and transport the injured to nearby hospitals, while police cordoned off the area to secure evidence. The explosion caused significant damage to the station’s façade and nearby storefronts, prompting a temporary suspension of police operations in the district.

Colombian officials launched a criminal investigation, with the National Police and the Attorney General’s Office confirming that the motive behind the attack remains under review. The incident occurs amid a broader pattern of violence linked to organized crime and insurgent groups that have targeted security forces across the country in recent years. Authorities have pledged to intensify security measures and pursue those responsible, while the government urged the public to remain vigilant as investigations continue.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Zelenskyy says Ukrainian drones will keep operating over Russia
content:
Kyiv’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Ukrainian drones will continue to operate over Russian territory, underscoring the ongoing aerial dimension of the conflict between the two nations. The statement was made amid a series of recent reports of unmanned aerial systems crossing the border, which Moscow has condemned as violations of its sovereign airspace.

Ukrainian officials have described the drone flights as part of a broader strategy to gather intelligence and conduct limited strikes against targets they deem militarily relevant, while Russian authorities have pledged to bolster air‑defence measures in response. Zelenskyy’s warning signals that Kyiv does not intend to curtail these operations despite diplomatic pressure, suggesting that the aerial component of the war will remain a persistent element of the hostilities.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Jurors deadlocked in Lindsay Clancy murder trial as judge urges continued deliberations
content:
A mother from Massachusetts has been formally charged with murder in connection with the deaths of her three children, who were found dead in the family’s residence in 2023. Prosecutors allege that the killings occurred within the home, prompting a criminal investigation that led to the filing of multiple homicide counts against the suspect. The case was brought before a district court, where the mother entered a plea of not guilty and was ordered to remain in custody pending further proceedings.

Law enforcement officials have not released additional specifics regarding the motive or the circumstances surrounding the incident, citing the ongoing nature of the investigation. The district attorney’s office indicated that a preliminary hearing is scheduled for later this year, at which the court will consider evidence and determine whether the case will proceed to trial. The charges underscore the seriousness of the alleged offenses and the legal process that will follow.
author: BBC World

title: US conducts additional strikes on Iran after accusations of targeting shipping and troops
content:
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) publicly accused Iran of deliberately targeting commercial vessels and American service members operating in the region, saying the actions represent a direct threat to maritime security and U.S. forces deployed abroad. The statement, released in response to a series of incidents over the past weeks, highlighted that Iranian forces have engaged in hostile activities aimed at disrupting trade routes and endangering personnel stationed in the area.

According to CENTCOM, the alleged attacks have taken place primarily in the Gulf and adjacent waters, where Iranian-backed militias have fired upon or attempted to seize merchant ships, and have conducted hostile maneuvers toward U.S. naval assets. The command noted that its forces have responded with defensive measures to protect both the commercial traffic and American troops, while continuing to monitor the situation closely. No casualties have been reported, but the incidents have prompted heightened alert levels among U.S. units in the theater.

The accusations come amid heightened regional tensions and ongoing diplomatic efforts to de‑escalate confrontations. U.S. officials indicated that the situation will be reviewed in coordination with allied partners, and that further actions may be taken to safeguard shipping lanes and service members if the threats persist. CENTCOM affirmed its commitment to maintaining freedom of navigation and the safety of personnel in the contested waters.
author: BBC World

title: Pioneer 11 becomes first spacecraft to fly by Saturn on Sept. 1, 1979
content:
On September 1, 1979, NASA’s robotic probe Pioneer 11 became the first spacecraft to perform a fly‑by of Saturn, marking a milestone in planetary exploration. Launched in 1973, Pioneer 11 had already visited Jupiter, providing the first close‑up images of the planet’s Great Red Spot and its ring system. The Saturn encounter followed a carefully planned trajectory that used a gravity assist from Jupiter to accelerate the probe to the speed needed for the outer‑planet fly‑by.

During the encounter, Pioneer 11 transmitted detailed data on Saturn’s atmosphere, rings, and moons, including the first close images of the planet’s faint rings and the discovery of the planet’s magnetic field. The probe also detected the presence of a faint, dusty ring around the moon Titan and measured the composition of Saturn’s upper atmosphere, confirming the presence of ammonia and water vapor. These observations provided the scientific community with unprecedented insight into the structure and dynamics of the Saturnian system and laid the groundwork for subsequent missions such as Voyager 2 and Cassini.

The successful fly‑by demonstrated the feasibility of deep‑space navigation and long‑duration communication, validating the technology and mission design that would be used for later probes. Pioneer 11’s data remain a valuable reference for planetary scientists, and its achievement is recognized as a pivotal moment in the history of space exploration, expanding humanity’s understanding of the outer planets and their complex environments.
author: Space.com

title: Brughmans joins Liverpool in deal worth up to £30m
content:
Liverpool Football Club has confirmed the acquisition of teenage goalkeeper Lucca Brughmans, with the transfer scheduled to take effect at the start of the 2027-28 season. The agreement represents a planned addition to the club’s youth development framework and aligns with ongoing efforts to secure long-term squad depth across all positions.

Brughmans joins the academy structure following an extensive evaluation by Liverpool’s scouting and performance departments, which prioritize identifying goalkeepers with the technical and physical attributes required for modern football. The club’s sporting leadership has indicated that the signing supports a broader recruitment model focused on integrating emerging talent into a structured progression pathway. All necessary administrative and medical procedures will be finalized ahead of the player’s official registration and reporting date.

The move underscores Liverpool’s continued commitment to youth infrastructure and forward-looking squad planning. Brughmans will begin training with the club’s development teams and participate in age-appropriate competitive fixtures as he
author: BBC Sport

title: ICE claims sufficient body cameras after series of officer-involved shootings
content:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officials are considering the deployment of cameras to improve transparency and accountability amid growing scrutiny of the agency’s record of violence. The proposal comes after a review of the Trump administration’s enforcement operations revealed that immigration officers were involved in more than two dozen shootings, raising concerns about the adequacy of oversight and the protection of detainee rights. By installing body‑mounted and fixed cameras at detention facilities and during field operations, ICE aims to create an objective record of interactions that could be used for internal investigations and public reporting.

The move follows a broader trend in federal law enforcement to adopt video‑surveillance technology as a deterrent to misconduct. Proponents argue that continuous recording would provide clear evidence in cases of alleged abuse, help train officers, and reassure the public that ICE is committed to lawful conduct. Critics, however, question whether cameras alone can address systemic issues such as training deficiencies and procedural inconsistencies. ICE officials have indicated that any new camera program would be phased in with pilot sites and accompanied by strict data‑management protocols to protect privacy while ensuring accountability.

If implemented, the camera initiative could mark a significant shift in ICE’s operational culture, offering a tangible tool to monitor compliance with federal regulations and reduce incidents of violence. The agency’s leadership has pledged to report on the program’s progress and to engage stakeholders—including civil‑rights groups and detention‑facility staff—in ongoing evaluation.
